### [Dystopia, Lived In: Adi Newton Talks Clock DVA Reissues White Souls in Black Suits & Thirst](link_21)

5 October 2026

by [James Broscheid](link_22)

“The live performances energized our situation and intensified it with lots of adrenaline and everything else. And on stage we used a lot of strobes and visual things like slide projections, so it was an assemblage of all these images and sounds coexisting. That does alienate the audience in some sense because you know they weren’t used to that kind of thing. It was new. People were expecting to see four guys on stage or whatever with instruments playing a whole selection of tracks or songs or whatever and that was it. We used to do a lot more with it.” – **Adi Newton** on **Clock DVA**’s early performances

[![Image 11](https://bigtakeover.com/images/38165.jpg)](https://bigtakeover.com/interviews/musical-machinations-a-quick-conversation-with-mattias-alsander-about-writing-songs-in-the-age-of-ai [link_23])

### [Musical Machinations: A quick conversation with Mattias Alsander about writing songs in the age of AI](link_23)

5 October 2026

by [Dave Franklin](link_24)

[![Image 12](https://bigtakeover.com/images/38140.jpg)](https://bigtakeover.com/interviews/summer-lovin-a-quick-chat-with-peter-jakobsson-about-love-songs-football-and-where-things-go-next [link_25])

### [Summer Lovin' : A quick chat with Peter Jakobsson about love songs, football and where things go next](link_25)

2 October 2026

by [Dave Franklin](link_24)

**Nautiluspete**, the project of Swedish songwriter **Peter Jakobsson** has just released a song about a love worth fighting for. “The Beacon” is uplifting EDM with a pop feel and a melodic drop. It felt like the perfect time to sit down with him to find out more about the song, his music and what the future holds.

[![Image 13](https://bigtakeover.com/images/38137.jpg)](https://bigtakeover.com/interviews/imperfect-on-purpose-buckets-capture-the-moment [link_26])

### [Imperfect on Purpose: Buckets Capture the Moment](link_26)

1 October 2026

by [James Broscheid](link_22)

“Big cities like L.A. are known for being very competitive when it comes to the music scene, but I think independent bands do have a duty to each other to help lift one another up, rather than try to ‘big dog’ each other. A thriving independent scene is good for everyone.” – **Mitch Rossiter**

“The first two records we did were all self-produced, and when I’m sitting alone in a room it’s easy to want to re-record everything one billion times until I lose the plot. They (Kyle Biane and Peter Recine) were also endlessly supportive no matter what instrument or idea we wanted to try.” – **Tanner Houghton**

[![Image 14](https://bigtakeover.com/images/38097.jpg)](https://bigtakeover.com/interviews/reflections-and-reality-modest-needs-on-healing-the-inner-child-and-making-music-as-its-own-reward [link_27])

### [Reflections and reality: Modest Needs on healing the inner child and making music as its own reward](link_27)

28 September 2026

by [Dave Franklin](link_24)

Modest Needs is the musical moniker of Thomas Modig, a singer-songwriter from Uppsala, Sweden, and with his reflective new single, ‘Ett bättre jag’ (‘A Better Me ‘), now out, it’s the perfect time to learn more about him and his music.

[![Image 15](https://bigtakeover.com/images/38087.jpg)](https://bigtakeover.com/interviews/interview-ian-haugland-europe [link_28])

### [Interview: Ian Haugland (Europe)](link_28)

25 September 2026

by [Chip Midnight](link_29)

Forty years after “The Final Countdown” put **Europe** on the map, the band’s full-throttle return to ’70s-inspired classic hard rock has cemented its place far beyond the hits that made it famous. Drummer **Ian Haugland** takes us inside _Come This Madness_ and a band that, four decades into its career, remains as interested in moving forward as it is reliving its past.

[![Image 16](https://bigtakeover.com/images/38091.jpg)](https://bigtakeover.com/interviews/a-star-is-born-a-chat-with-sean-macleod-about-the-new-album-and-the-freedom-of-not-overthinking-things [link_30])

### [A Star is Born: A chat with Sean MacLeod about the new album and the freedom of not overthinking things](link_30)

25 September 2026

by [Dave Franklin](link_24)

With a new album, the wonderfully titled _That’s When The Earth Becomes a Star_ just dropped, it felt like the perfect time to sit down with **Sean McLeod** to find out about his past, the current album, and what the future might hold.

[![Image 17](https://bigtakeover.com/images/38082.jpg)](https://bigtakeover.com/interviews/interview-dave-marr-and-philip-mcardle-the-star-room-boys [link_31])

### [Interview: Dave Marr and Philip McArdle (The Star Room Boys)](link_31)

25 September 2026

by [Chip Midnight](link_29)

A timeless-sounding country album, _Why Do Lonely Men and Women Want to Break Each Other’s Hearts?_ by Athens’ **The Star Room Boys** is being reissued for the first time on vinyl by **Strolling Bones Records**. **Dave Marr** and **Philip McArdle** share why now was the right time to revisit the album, the thrill of performing live again, and how a record originally released in 1999 sounds as if it could have come out today.

[![Image 18](https://bigtakeover.com/images/38044.jpg)](https://bigtakeover.com/interviews/keeping-it-real-the-real-anthem-on-genre-geography-and-what-makes-the-band-work-so-well [link_32])

### [Keeping it Real: The Real Anthem on genre, geography and what makes the band work so well](link_32)

22 September 2026

by [Dave Franklin](link_24)

With two singles now out ahead of an album to follow, it was the perfect time to sit down with **Matt King**, **Andy Mitchell** and **Shawn Helton** of **The Real Anthem** to find out how the band came about, what the new album will be all about and where things go next.

[![Image 19](https://bigtakeover.com/images/38039.jpg)](https://bigtakeover.com/interviews/a-beautiful-way-to-come-apart-mute-swan-and-skin-slip [link_33])

### [A Beautiful Way to Come Apart: Mute Swan and ‘Skin Slip’](link_33)

20 September 2026

by [James Broscheid](link_22)

“We agreed pretty quickly we were going to try to give it as big a release as possible no matter how much time and energy it took. A big part of that decision was our love for Thom. I don’t know if any of us believe he’s watching down on us but there is that thought and maybe that was a motivation.” – **Mike Barnett**

[![Image 20](https://bigtakeover.com/images/38033.png)](https://bigtakeover.com/interviews/interview-frank-bello-anthrax [link_34])

### [Interview: Frank Bello (Anthrax)](link_34)

18 September 2026

by [Chip Midnight](link_29)

**Anthrax** spent a decade away, then came back to record _Cursum Perficio_ at **Dave Grohl**’s **Studio 606**, where Grohl would wander in mid-session and start headbanging. Bassist **Frank Bello** talks about the long road to one of the best albums of the band’s career, and why he’s not done yet.

[![Image 21](https://bigtakeover.com/images/38016.png)](https://bigtakeover.com/interviews/interview-beth-plumb-and-dan-elliott-tokyo-tea-room [link_35])

### [Interview: Beth Plumb and Dan Elliott (Tokyo Tea Room)](link_35)

16 September 2026

by [Chip Midnight](link_29)

**Tokyo Tea Room**’s dreamy, groove-heavy dance-pop has found a surprising second life, with streaming algorithms helping older songs rack up tens of millions of listens and bringing renewed attention to the English band. **Beth Plumb** and **Dan Elliott** talk about the band’s new album _Feel Forever_, their successful U.S. tour, and this new chapter in Tokyo Tea Room’s story.

[![Image 22](https://bigtakeover.com/images/38001.jpg)](https://bigtakeover.com/interviews/interview-the-family [link_36])

### [Interview: The Family](link_36)

14 September 2026

by [Chip Midnight](link_29)

With a sound not unlike ’70s-era **Fleetwood Mac**, **The Family**’s debut album, _Delusions of Grandeur_, nearly never saw the light of day. Written and recorded during the pandemic by members of a blended family with impressive musical resumes, the album sat unreleased until yet another family connection stepped in to bring it to listeners. **James** and **Dylan LeBlanc**, **Angela Hacker**, and **Bay Simpson** discuss the album’s star-crossed beginning and what it means to finally have it out in the world.

[![Image 23](https://bigtakeover.com/images/37997.jpg)](https://bigtakeover.com/interviews/the-space-between-margaret-glaspy-on-i-am-both [link_37])

### [The Space Between: Margaret Glaspy on I Am Both](link_37)

14 September 2026

by [James Broscheid](link_22)

“I think music is such a beautiful reflection of what America is—it comes from everywhere, from all over the world.” – **Margaret Glaspy**

[![Image 24](https://bigtakeover.com/images/37983.jpg)](https://bigtakeover.com/interviews/finding-meaning-in-the-mess-rowena-wise-on-bad-things-feel-good [link_38])

### [Finding Meaning in the Mess: Rowena Wise on ‘Bad Things Feel Good*'](link_38)

11 September 2026

by [James Broscheid](link_22)

“Maybe adulthood isn’t about finally understanding yourself. Maybe it’s more about developing enough trust in yourself that you can survive not knowing, and enough compassion for your past selves that you don’t need to keep putting them on trial. I like the idea that we never really arrive, that we just get a little better at travelling with ourselves.” – **Rowena Wise**

[![Image 25](https://bigtakeover.com/images/37954.jpg)](https://bigtakeover.com/interviews/interview-lily-seabird [link_39])

### [Interview: Lily Seabird](link_39)

4 September 2026

by [Chip Midnight](link_29)

**Lily Seabird**’s _Lightspheres on Their Way_ is the best thing she’s ever made which is saying something. For now, it’s a reward reserved for those willing to track down the vinyl or CD, streaming arriving next month. On the eve of her UK tour, Seabird talks about the record, the Burlington, Vermont music scene, and the notebooks from which the lyrics were born.

[![Image 26](https://bigtakeover.com/images/37911.jpg)](https://bigtakeover.com/interviews/interview-maoli [link_40])

### [Interview: Maoli](link_40)

29 August 2026

by [Katherine Yeske Taylor](link_41)

Hawaiian reggae-country superstar **Maoli** discusses his new album _MMO3_, how he went from being a laborer to one of Hawaii’s most acclaimed musicians, and why he thinks his music has connected with listeners even beyond his native Maui

[![Image 27](https://bigtakeover.com/images/37909.jpg)](https://bigtakeover.com/interviews/interview-austin-wilson-convinced-friend [link_42])

### [Interview: Austin Wilson (Convinced Friend)](link_42)

28 August 2026

by [Chip Midnight](link_29)

On **Convinced Friend**’s sophomore album, _Nowhere Songs_, **Austin Wilson** channels influences ranging from the Louisiana oilfields where he grew up to the Americana-folk spirit of **Counting Crows**, resulting in a captivating collection of story-driven songs that exist somewhere between memory, myth, and reality.

[![Image 28](https://bigtakeover.com/images/37873.jpg)](https://bigtakeover.com/interviews/interview-puddles-pity-party [link_43])

### [Interview: Puddles Pity Party](link_43)

23 August 2026

by [Katherine Yeske Taylor](link_41)

**Mike Geier** – the man behind **Puddles Pity Party** – discusses the clown with the golden voice who is endearing himself to audiences around the world

[![Image 29](https://bigtakeover.com/images/37868.jpg)](https://bigtakeover.com/interviews/interview-john-ross-wild-pink [link_44])

### [Interview: John Ross (Wild Pink)](link_44)

20 August 2026

by [Chip Midnight](link_29)

Another **Wild Pink** album worthy of “album of the year” consideration, **John Ross**’s songwriting blends the Tom Petty influence instilled as a kid growing up in Florida with Bruce Springsteen’s working class ethos. That combination has made him one of the defining voices of heartland indie rock, standing alongside peers MJ Lenderman, Fust, and Big Thief.

[![Image 30](https://bigtakeover.com/images/37798.jpg)](https://bigtakeover.com/interviews/interview-kelly-doyle [link_45])

### [Interview: Kelly Doyle](link_45)

14 August 2026

by [Chip Midnight](link_29)

Best known for backing artists like **Phosphorescent** and **Robert Ellis**, guitarist **Kelly Doyle** steps into the spotlight with _Thieves_, an album that feels less like a standard jazz record and more like a lost film soundtrack. In this conversation with the Houston musician, Doyle discusses cinematic songwriting, vintage influences, and the art of tone.

[![Image 31](https://bigtakeover.com/images/37786.jpg)](https://bigtakeover.com/interviews/interview-johanna-samuels [link_46])

### [Interview: Johanna Samuels](link_46)

14 August 2026

by [Chip Midnight](link_29)

Combining an intimate ’70s Laurel Canyon warmth with the distinctive chord changes of early-aughts songwriting, **Johanna Samuels**’ _Sorry, Kid_, is a modern take on nostalgia, a collection of songs with a history spanning decades. ### [Interview: Eugene San (Go With Strangers)](https://bigtakeover.com/interviews/InterviewEugeneSanGoWithStrangers)

[![Image 10: Eugene San of Go With Strangers](https://bigtakeover.com/images/25279.jpg)](https://bigtakeover.com/images/25279.jpg)

31 July 2022

by [Jen Dan](https://bigtakeover.com/author/Jen+Dan/)

Eugene San of Go With Strangers, exclusive to Big Takeover – Photo Credit: Freya Pang

A few months ago I had the opportunity to conduct the following interview with **Eugene San**, the mastermind behind dynamic and dreamy alternative rock music project **Go With Strangers**. The Malaysian musician, songwriter, and singer has a long history in the music field, previously founding the outfits **Kojira**, **Gene Shanzo**, and **Mint Cherry**.

Now as Go With Strangers, San brings in sweeping, scintillating, and expansive guitars, rich and miasmic electronic textures, and placidly contemplative vocals for a captivating sonic experience. His debut record as Go With Strangers, _Finding Ikigai_ EP, is self-released and out now.

Parts of this interview can be found exclusively in the latest print edition of Big Takeover magazine, issue #90 with Billy Bragg on the cover.

[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wHzASxMX7gw)

**Hello Eugene! It’s so exciting to find out more about you and your music. Before we go into all that, where are you based now, and how has the pandemic been treating you?**

Hi Jen! Thank you so much. I’m based in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. Been here all my life. The pandemic hit us hard, especially for the service and entertainment industry, due to the lockdowns.

Even now, many live venues over here are having a hard time (and also given a hard time), due to restrictions for live shows. But personally, I work mostly from home, so I’m grateful for still being able to do what I usually do.

**I’m swooning over your new _Finding Ikigai_ EP as the music project Go With Strangers. But you’re actually no stranger to the music realm. I don’t know the details about your past output, so can you go a bit into the previous bands you’ve been in and projects you’re associated with?**

I’ve been in a few bands and projects over the time, but the most significant ones for me started with a band named **Kojira** (alternative-metal/grunge), we managed to get an album out before it ended.

I then wandered into mellower music, and made a simple album for a modern classical/ambient project called **Gene Shanzo**; before letting that one go and venturing into electronic/indie-pop music with a group called **Mint Cherry**.

**What compelled you to start up your new project Go With Strangers?**

It all started with a cover that I did on Mogwai’s “Ritchie Sacramento”, last year, during one of the lockdowns. I was still new to post-rock and shoegaze music then. Before that, I had been itching to make heavier music again.

And coincidentally, somewhere around that time, Mint Cherry was also evolving from ‘synthesizer-laden’ electro-pop, to more ‘band-oriented’ indie-pop type of music. I think everything sort of fell into place at the right time…

I believe I have Mogwai to thank for releasing “Ritchie Sacramento” at such a good timing too. Haha!

**How did the pandemic influence the creation of your new EP? Under what conditions did you record the EP (home studio or…?)?**

_Finding Ikigai_ EP was recorded in my home “studio” (Well, home office). I am definitely not a professional mixing sound-engineer at all by any means, and I think if a professional sound-engineer were to analyze this EP, it may probably be a mess. Haha! … But if it is really a mess, may it be a sonic mess… I am just grateful to be able to make it all work for the EP, and the sound I wanted to achieve in this EP.

**_Finding Ikigai_ is breathtaking in its rich and propulsive sound, and also its carefully crafted song structures. You call the songs “alternative rock,” but I would call them dream-rock, or maybe the dynamic side of shoegaze. Do you agree that maybe your music could be described that way too?**

All I could think of my music was just rock. It’s not hard rock, nor metal. And, hmm.. Shoegaze… I’m still on the fence about that. I do know the dedicated shoegaze community has a certain concept of what proper shoegaze should sound like, and I understand that.

I have absolutely nothing but love, respect and appreciation for the shoegaze community listeners and supporters; but even then, I still do not think my music is shoegaze.

There are better modern bands out there doing the proper shoegaze work, bands like Whimsical, Quietly Into The Night, etc. I also heard of another term for modern/newer shoegaze called ‘nu-gaze’, but even then, there are some die-hard shoegazers who despise this term ‘nu-gaze’, and my music isn’t exactly ‘nu-gaze’ either.

So I still believe that ‘alternative’-rock should be the closest to it. ‘Dream-rock’ could also be a good one. Haha!

[Video 2](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGCQ3iqBaCg)

**Speaking of which, tell us why you got into this alternative rock sound, which is different from what you’ve released in the past.**

About why it is different – I think the past music projects, and also some things that happened along the way in my life, were the main turning points that shaped the music I needed to create and express now, at this point of my life, in Go With Strangers.

**The EP recently came out, and before that you’d released two sublime singles with dreamy accompanying music videos. What has the reception been like?**

The reception has been really heart-warming and humbling so far. Seeing and feeling the love and support from listeners, and people I’ve never even met before, from around the world and across the other ends of this earth.. It’s surreal. Almost like a dream.

I also really need to thank **Mark Anderson** from Static Sounds Club for being super-cool and supportive from the start, and propelling the premiere of my first music video “Further”. The awesome DJs at DKFM Shoegaze Radio, one of the main radio stations that is actually actively supporting the shoegaze music scene across the world. (I also have them to thank for confusing me about the type of music I’m making. Haha!). And your good self for the support all the way since I started this project.

**_The Little Prince_ -inspired video is especially poignant for “Slow Down, Wild One.” Did you envision the video, or was that the work of the director or…?**

I’m actually quite surprised that you mentioned _Little Prince’_ As I’ve actually never seen this comic/cartoon before, only after a friend told me that the boy looked like the character from the Chinese version of _Little Prince_ (apparently there’s a Chinese version of _Little Prince_ too). only did I start Googling and finding illustrations/photos of the boy with the scarf, sitting on the globe.

When I was exploring different ideas on the best approach to create the video for “Slow Down, Wild One,” I came across a director, and his video work.

One of his works [was] footage of a boy, protecting a rose, until it grew into a large rose, in a outer-space sort of environment. The original footage was quite raw, and did not have the ‘sand-storm’ effect yet. I really liked the metaphor of this boy watching over, and protecting his rose (little one), until it grew up.

With permission, I got the footage, shot my own footage, and edited them all together into a story-flow. Am really happy with how the video turned out.

**What’s next up your sleeve? Any more videos? Are there plans for a full length album? I dearly hope so!**

Initially the plan was to gig after the EP release, with the support of a few friends as my live bandmates. But due to the current on-going restrictions for live shows over here, and also the rising Covid cases, I’m not sure when that would be happening.

An album is definitely on my list, but at the moment, I’m just taking some time off writing.

I’ve actually picked up skateboarding again! Picking up where I left off 20 years ago, relearning even the most basic tricks again. The body is not taking it as well as before though. Haha! But it feels great to be doing it again, even though not as gnarly as before.

[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nkmQXHg95ps)

### [Song Premiere: "Something I Like" by Meyru](https://bigtakeover.com/news/SongPremiereSomethingILikebyMeyru)

[![Image 10: Meyru](https://bigtakeover.com/images/20950.jpg)](https://bigtakeover.com/images/20950.jpg)

22 May 2019

by [Jen Dan](https://bigtakeover.com/author/Jen+Dan/)

Meyru – Photo Credit: Ari Weiss

NYC-based trio **Meyru** (made up of two cousins and a life-long friend) treats listeners with their fresh take on nostalgic indie rock/pop and are doing it again with their new single. “Something I Like”, which is the second release from their forthcoming album _Good To See You_ arriving this summer.

The band spent a month in the mountains of North Carolina where they recorded their debut LP in the basement of an abandoned church with the help of Brooklyn-located producer **Tyler Brown** and mastering engineer **Dan Millice** (A$AP Rocky, Al Green, 50 Cent).

Meyru’s indie pop melodies, bolstered by intricate rock guitar leads and driving bass has led them to a series of sold-out shows at NYC venues including the Mercury Lounge, The Bowery Electric, Pianos, and The Bitter End.

Following previous hit “Running Day Dreams,” Meyru takes their sound to the next level on the fiery “Something I Like”. They’ve perfected the balance between subdued and energetic indie rock that’s uninhibited and in-your-face, but still laid-back.

The band brings a fervent energy to this smoldering, bass-driven track, which The Big Takeover is pleased to premiere here. Powered by a relentless bass line and emphatic drum strikes, “Something I Like” also adds fast-strummed guitar jags, raspy, rousing vocals, and light vocal harmonies on the chorus sections. Meyru definitely have something we like!

The band members comment, _““Something I Like” is a song we wrote after a long weekend of partying in Montreal with our friends that lived there at the time. On the surface the song is about driving through the night to make it back to NYC in time for our day jobs at 9am. But the song really describes trying to shake the comedown of a weekend high, as well as the feelings you have for a person after just a few nights, all while trying to stay awake at the wheel and make it back to the real world.”_

### [Hatchie: Lost in the Dream](https://bigtakeover.com/profiles/hatchie)

[![Image 10](https://bigtakeover.com/images/37413.jpg)](https://bigtakeover.com/images/37413.jpg)

20 July 2026

by [Susan Moll](https://bigtakeover.com/author/Susan+Moll/)

Photo by Bianca Edwards

In his 2021 book titled _The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows_, author **John Koenig** identified an intriguing phenomenon known as anemoia, which he defines as a unique form of nostalgia in which one aches, painfully, for a time or place one has never actually known, and memories of experiences never actually lived. Melbourne’s **Hatchie** (born Harriette Pilbeam) has caught a serious case of it. “I think music can unlock memories,” she confides. “I think it’s my teenage years and my early 20s that I really find I’m most nostalgic for. It’s not necessarily that I want to go back to them, it’s more just like something can instantly transport me back there. I think that’s really fascinating.”

On _Liquorice_ (Secretly Canadian), her third album as **Hatchie**, Pilbeam captures that energy and runs with it. She breathes life into “Anemoia” with a passionate sigh, opening the album on a beguiling note. A sweet-faced strawberry blonde of 33 with an easy laugh and a radiant warmth, she still cherishes the sounds of her girlhood. “I think music can really take me back to being a teenager,” she says. “I think I often wonder about all of the different moments, like the butterfly effect moments that my life could have been completely different if I did or didn’t discover certain music.”

Though Pilbeam confesses she’s a “more a dream pop lover than a shoegaze lover” at present, she’s always infused plenty of shoegaze-oriented moments into **Hatchie**’s discography. _Liquorice_ is no different. “Wonder” launches heavenward to Souvlaki Space Station as she channels echoes of **Slowdive**, **My Bloody Valentine** and **Chapterhouse** through a prism all her own. **Yuck**, **Cocteau Twins**, **Cleaners from Venus** and **Wild Nothing** also count among Pilbeam’s favorites.

“Yesterday, I was listening to **Wild Nothing**’s first EP, and that instantly took me back to being a teenager,” she reveals. “I distinctly remember being in my bedroom listening to it with fairy lights on my roof and all the lights off, spending my whole Saturday night discovering new music and feeling I had a whole new personality based on that music. I think it’s my teenage years and my early 20s that I really find I’m most nostalgic for. It’s not necessarily that I want to go back to them, it’s more just like something can instantly transport me back there.”

Memories remain a powerful catalyst for Pilbeam as she revisits the past she longs for. She was summering with friends in upstate New York when the new sounds that evolved into _Liquorice_ first surfaced. “I had started writing a few ideas for the album, but nothing was really working,” she laments. “I was also really quite unhappy and quite dissatisfied with a few elements of my life, and I think I was just leaning into that feeling. I was looking up stuff about nostalgia and all the feelings I was having. I think I looked up missing someone you don’t know or missing something you haven’t experienced yet, and it came up with that. That really struck a chord with me.”

Nostalgia is a tie that binds _Liquorice_ from beginning to end; on “Someone Else’s News,” Pilbeam yearns, as we all have at one point or another, to “rip it up and start again.” On the fanciful “Only One Laughing,” she laments, “I never knew that what once excited me wasn’t what’s meant to be.” For everything that wasn’t meant to be for Pilbeam there’s plenty that was, namely her relationship with longtime personal and musical partner Joe Agius, whom she wed in Las Vegas in 2021. (Is it heaven or Las Vegas? We may never know.)

“We’ve been working together for so long that we really have a shorthand for what we want to do with songs,” Pilbeam confides. “We’re really good at not stepping on each other’s toes. I think we just get it. I think we click. What we originally connected over was music, so that’s always been this common thread between us. We’re like a Venn diagram that crosses over, so working on this music is really that sweet spot right in the middle.”

The couple’s bond further deepened as they migrated to Los Angeles to record _Liquorice_ with Jay Som’s Melina Duterte. “Working with Jay Som was great,” enthuses Pilbeam. “She’s super warm and caring, and that’s exactly what I wanted going into this. I wanted to work with someone who was a musician themselves in a band and had a similar experience to me. I just love that she’s a classic indie rock guitarist as well, so she added some really great shimmery guitars to the mix. We just had a lot of fun together.”

The relaxed vibe of the _Liquorice_ sessions gave Pilbeam a perfect opportunity to explore her intimate side. “This one is a lot more romantic and sensual,” she muses, sipping coffee on this rainy Monday morning. “I really wanted it to tell the stories that I haven’t told about falling in and out of love when I was younger. It took a lot of inspiration from external sources as well, watching a lot of romantic movies and going back over those times in my life.”

Helmed by a vast group of co-producers and co-writers, **Hatchie**’s 2022 breakthrough, _Giving the World Away_, evoked the Nineties sounds that so profoundly inspired Pilbeam in her youth. The record scored her a Stateside hit with “Lights On,” a moment of clarity for an artist coming into her own. For the cover art, the photogenic Pilbeam posed in leather and a set of angel wings reminiscent of **Baz Luhrmann**’s Juliet, an urban princess at one with the night. While _Giving the World Away_ put **Hatchie** on the map internationally, she now views it through a different lens. “I did really work those songs really, really hard to the point where maybe they were overworked,” she reminisces. “I think listening back, there are a few songs that I always put too much effort into.”

By comparison, there’s a distinctly Spartan quality to _Liquorice_. Guitar effects and dissonance aside, each song delivers a clarifying sense of purity. “I really wanted this album, sonically, to be as simple as possible,” explains Pilbeam, “whereas with my previous album, I think I was really trying to prove that I could do something as complex as possible and as experimental for me as possible. This one, I tried to do the complete opposite and just slow down and work with my abilities.”

And Pilbeam’s abilities are legion, particularly her inventive knack for harmony, her dulcet singing voice and her effervescent joie de vivre. But _Liquorice_ isn’t all sweetness and light, especially with respect to “Part That Bleeds,” a moody reverie that recalls a painful breakup: “We were written as a tragedy.” But the intervening years have been generous to Hatchie, bolstering Pilbeam’s confidence and building her creative strength. _Liquorice_ offers a uniquely absorbing gaze into a multifaceted heart.

“I think I love how much of it is me,” she marvels. “Only ‘Lose it Again’ and ‘Carousel’ were songs that I fully cowrote with other people, and all the other ones are songs that I wrote pretty much fully. I really like that it feels totally mine. I know that I didn’t compromise at all with this one. I really stuck to my guns. I wanted it to sound fuzzy and DIY and romantic and emotional and sensual and a little more grown-up than my last album. I feel like I really did what I set out to do. I’m just really proud of that.”

# Kazdoura Slows Down Time on Hypnotic Psych-Rock Track ‘Ala Mahlak’

The Arabic psych-rock duo urge listeners to slow down and savour the moment on their latest single 'Ala Mahlak' from their upcoming album,'Markab', released via Habibi Funk Records.

[Scene Noise](https://scenenoise.com/WriterProfile/5215)

Oct 05, 2026

![Image 6: Kazdoura Slows Down Time on Hypnotic Psych-Rock Track ‘Ala Mahlak’](https://scenenoise.com/Content/Articles/Big_image/a1b35e3c-3e26-41c9-b408-0c29a1ce0659.jpg)

Toronto-based Arabic psych-rock duo Kazdoura offer a gentle plea to linger in the present moment on their latest single, ‘Ala Mahlak’. Warm and laid-back, the track urges listeners to step back from the rush of modern life, encouraging a slower pace both lyrically and sonically.It serves as an inviting preview of their upcoming album,'Markab', set for release on December 4th via Habibi Funk Records.

The production breathes with a sun-drenched, vintage aesthetic, woven together by velvety vocals, jazz-influenced chord progressions, and a dynamic arrangement. A funky bassline pairs with precise drum work to establish a steady, swaying pulse, while gentle flutes enrich the harmonic foundation. Halfway through, the song pivots into a more rhythmically charged second half, driven by swirling wah-wah guitars that fully embrace the duo’s psychedelic sensibilities.

This desire to suspend time comes alive through simple, intimate lyrics that vividly capture the warmth of a late-summer evening: lazily rolling cigarettes, listening to easygoing music, and simply living without a care in the world.

### [Interview: Puddles Pity Party](https://bigtakeover.com/interviews/interview-puddles-pity-party)

[![Image 10](https://bigtakeover.com/images/37873.jpg)](https://bigtakeover.com/images/37873.jpg)

23 August 2026

by [Katherine Yeske Taylor](https://bigtakeover.com/author/Katherine+Yeske+Taylor/)

Photo by David Stuart

It’s undoubtedly safe to say that **Puddles Pity Party** is one of the most original acts you’re likely to find. A 6’8” clown with an astounding voice (but who is mute otherwise), he is at once formidable and endearing. Known for his emotive and innovative covers of a wildly disparate collection of cover songs – including “War Pigs” by **Black Sabbath**, “Royals* by **Lorde**, “Where Is My Mind?” by **Pixies**, and many more – he has also just released an album of original material, _No One’s Free_, which can be bought or streamed at the outlets listed here: [puddles.lnk.to/links](https://puddles.lnk.to/links)

Puddles is based in Atlanta, but he’s currently in the midst of an extensive North American tour as the opening act for **Weird Al” Yankovic**. He is also planning his own headlining tour starting next February, with dates TBA. Besides showcasing his extraordinary voice, these shows highlight his penchant for offbeat humor and lots of audience interaction, as well.

**Mike Geier**, the man behind Puddles (or, if you will, Puddles’ “representative”) recently spoke with _The Big Takeover_ about the new album, winning over skeptical audience members, and how Puddles has affected him – and others.

_For anyone reading this who does not know who Puddles is, can you give an overview?_

MIKE GEIER: I mean, there’s the obvious: Puddles is a clown. Puddles is a clown that feels everything, and sort of indulges in feeling everything, and often expresses himself through a song and also interaction with an audience. All of these different feelings, and all of these phases of how people feel things – and it’s all things. He’s often been called a sad clown. He’s sad sometimes. But he’s not only sad. He’s not only happy. He’s not only absurd. He’s all of those things simultaneously. I’ve always resisted trying to explain Puddles because the moment I say something, it’s like, “Well, that’s not really it, either.” From his perspective, Puddles is like, “I don’t care; say whatever you want.” He’s going to do what he wants. So I’m not trying to be difficult or obtuse or anything about it, but it’s hard to describe. But also, I think that not everything needs an explanation, which kind of goes against a lot of things, especially if commerce is related to it. There’s so many dimensions to it. I feel like it’s something you really have to experience firsthand [at a show].

[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WT8t3i8CkMQ)

_Normally, performers tell stories between songs, and talk with the audience – but because Puddles doesn’t speak, only sings, is it ever difficult to get his point across?_

MIKE GEIER: He, and we, try to create mechanisms through song, and also the way Puddles will deliver a song. And visuals. And also, I think establishing a rapport with an audience early on. There are these bullet points that he likes to hit, but he likes to begin with, “Okay, this is going to be weird,” and then begins in earnest in authentically presenting these emotional themes. So Puddles has no problem with any of that sort of navigating or negotiating, “Am I being understood or not?” Because Puddles also believes that, “You guys are with it. You showed up here, so you must be curious and you want to know about this.” So we give the audience lots and lots of credit for being already halfway there when he begins. So I think establishing kind of an absurdity right off the top allows Puddles to do it his way. He doesn’t worry about making sure anyone understands. He believes that you’re going to understand.

_The biggest news in Puddles’ world is this new album. How did he know it was the right time to do one with original material instead of continuing to do cover songs?_

MIKE GEIER: **Andrew Douglas Quinn** is the songwriter of all these songs, and he’s a dear friend of ours. And I work with some other guys that worked with him for many years, other musicians, and **Tim Delaney**, who engineered the record and played on quite a bit of it, was in a band with Andrew. We were having this conversation one day about Andrew’s songs. One of the guys, **Brad Lewis**, who is one of the producers of it, said, “I hear Puddles singing these songs.” A lot of the songs that Puddles has done in the past are very recognizable covers, but when Puddles first started being known to people, quite a bit of his material were not well known covers. They were interpretations of songs of people that he or I knew, [such as] **Glyn Styler** from New Orleans, and **Dexter Romweber** of **Flat Duo Jets**, who was a friend of ours. Those were the songs, and they were interpretations of these songs, I think much in the tradition of **Linda Ronstadt**, for example. Linda Ronstadt did other people’s songs in these brilliant ways. She was an interpreter of songs, and I feel the same way about **Frank Sinatra** and **Barbra Streisand**. **Céline Dion** is an interpreter of songs, as well. So we kind of looked at it in that way, as opposed to “cover artist.” So we’re doing these things, a **David Bowie** song or a **Queen** song or whatever, and Brad was like, “Why don’t we do Andrew’s songs? They’re brilliant songs.” And so we approached Andrew, and he agreed with it. So we said, “We’re just going to take them and run with them.” And we did, and we discovered that a lot of the elements in the songs didn’t really need that much interpreting. He has all of these pop sensibilities, and those are things that Puddles hasn’t really explored that much in the past, so it was a great opportunity to take some creative and artistic risks, and also change it up musically from what has happened before. The other thing is, thematically, these songs fit nicely within Puddles’ idea of feelings. Personal relationship feelings, but also relationships within culture, especially culture within this country.

[Video 2](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tGJIjhCWMmI)

_How did Puddles realize he had such an exceptional voice in the first place?_

MIKE GEIER: You know, it just came out. And a lot of experimenting happened along the way. There’s a term that we like to use called “failing forward.” It’s about the potential for failure, and also actually failing, and through that process, discovering new perspectives. Or, it often will steel your resolve about, “Okay, I tried doing it a different way and it blew up in my face. The way I was doing it [before] was the right way.” Or you discover a new way of doing things. It seems like a fundamental process to me, in that way.

_Is it vindicating when Puddles has won over a skeptical audience?_

MIKE GEIER: The thing about Puddles is, he’s very sensitive. He wears his feeling on his sleeve; you can tell how Puddles feels about things. But he [also] has this quality that is a little, “Oh yeah? Hold my beer” type of idea. And I think the audience having doubts or reservations, that’s energy they’re bringing in from the outside world, which is a protective thing that we do. We get in a car and we put on the seat belt and the red light and all this stuff that’s going on every second of us being out in the world, and we have to have this armor. So you park the car, you go into the venue, and all of that is coming with you. And Puddles is super aware of that. So his idea is, “I’m just going to do the thing and let’s give the audience a chance to catch up.” And it just seems to work. Some people walk away and it’s not their bag. That’s totally cool. And some take longer than others. But there was definitely an indulgent sense of euphoria when Puddles finished his show at **Madison Square Garden** and they all stood up and it kind of freaked him out. He gets very emotional in those moments. That’s what happened on AGT when the audience cheered. [Puddles appeared on the 12th season of the _America’s Got Talent_ television show, in 2017.] I can imagine it was pretty weird for the audience: “Wow, what’s this going on? Who’s this stupid goon on stage? What’s he going to do?” And then that happened and they accepted him. They felt it. And so he gets very emotional about that. So there’s more of a sense of, sometimes I use the word fellowship, but I don’t mean it in like a religious way. I mean, everybody gets connected.

[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xhmYI84d4io)

_I’m glad to get the word out about this album and Puddles in general, because I feel like more people should know about him. I think the world needs more empathy and understanding, and I think that Puddles is good for that._

MIKE GEIER: I couldn’t agree with you more. I feel like Puddles is just doing what Puddles does. I’ve very intimate knowledge of everything [he does], and it still feels like, “Where is this going?” And I try to stay out of its way. I just let Puddles go where Puddles needs to go, and I just want to play a supportive role in doing that. But I’ve learned a whole bunch of stuff from doing this, and I think it’s affected me in an incredible, positive way, especially when it comes to understanding and inclusivity and empathy and compassion. I don’t have any suggestions for how anyone else is supposed to do anything in their life. I just know how it makes me feel through all of these experiences that I would have never experienced without Puddles. It’s pretty incredible.

![Image 11](https://bigtakeover.com/images/37874.png)

# Nour Chehab Weaves Melancholy Into Guitar-Driven Single ‘Jaloux'

The Lebanese singer-songwriter blends kinetic drum grooves with wistful melodies and layered guitar work on her latest single.

[Scene Noise](https://scenenoise.com/WriterProfile/5215)

Oct 05, 2026

![Image 6: Nour Chehab Weaves Melancholy Into Guitar-Driven Single ‘Jaloux'](https://scenenoise.com/Content/Articles/Big_image/2f5b21f7-ffe8-484e-a3f6-b3e87860f5e7.jpg)

Beirut-based singer-songwriter and multi-instrumentalist Nour Chehab steps into her solo spotlight with her debut single, ‘Jaloux’.

Chehab has built a following on Instagram through Oud covers of contemporary pop songs. On ‘Jaloux’, however, she switches to guitar, an instrument she has played since the age of seven. The track draws on that longstanding connection, pairing her acoustic guitar work with locked-in drum grooves and bright melodies that give the song an easy, upbeat bounce, while a thread of wistfulness runs beneath its breezy surface.

Driven by a live drum kit and delicate electric textures, the production sets up a lively call-and-response between crisp guitar licks and Chehab’s soulful French vocals. Luminous harmonies soften the track’s quick tempo, giving it a dreamy, sweeping quality without losing its danceable pulse.

‘Jaloux’ ultimately finds its balance in the space between pop sensibilities and Chehab’s musicianship, using a rhythmic, guitar-led arrangement to introduce an artist whose sound feels both carefully crafted and instinctive.

# MOUSV Turns His Daily Routine into Brash Anthem on ‘Kol Youm’

The Egyptian rapper tackles daily struggles on ‘Kol Youm’, blending energetic hip-hop with neon-drenched nocturnal visuals.

[Scene Noise](https://scenenoise.com/WriterProfile/5215)

Oct 01, 2026

![Image 6: MOUSV Turns His Daily Routine into Brash Anthem on ‘Kol Youm’](https://scenenoise.com/Content/Articles/Big_image/72d0e618-83a0-4397-a936-4f8bfbea57b5.jpg)

Stepping into a shadowy soundscape, Egyptian artist MOUSV tackles the weight of the daily grind on his latest single, ‘Kol Youm’. Channeling vibrant, synth-heavy sonics, the track reimagines MOUSV’s day-to-day through a boastful, contemporary lens.

At the centre of the arrangement, producer Danny crafts a fluid, forward-thinking beat that pairs kinetic rhythms with an ever-shifting energy. Across this dense backdrop, MOUSV retains full command, balancing his sharp penmanship with an adaptable vocal presence. Zozrealstar’s mix and Marwan Sami’s mastering give the instrumental plenty of breathing room, keeping its intricate textures polished without dampening its raw punch.

The track’s thematic weight extends seamlessly into its visual treatment, directed by Abdelrahman El Morsi. Frame by frame, El Morsi immerses MOUSV in a sprawling, neon-drenched metropolis, capturing the artist wandering alone through quiet nighttime corridors. The video operates as a cinematic extension of the music itself, channeling the quiet isolation and friction of urban survival into a stark, stylised world.

[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qoRrosSc90g)

في «كل يوم»، يدخل موسي إلى مساحة موسيقية مختلفة، متناولًا صراعات الحياة اليومية وتفاصيلها من خلال هيب هوب حديث وحماسي. ويأتي التراك متأثرًا بالاتجاه الموسيقي الذي انتشر في الولايات المتحدة خلال الفترة الأخيرة، خصوصًا في أعمال Lil Yachty، وهو صوت بدأ يترك أثره على المشهد الموسيقي المصري أيضًا.

يقود المنتج داني التوزيع في اتجاه متماسك ومتطور، يجمع بين الطاقة والإيقاعات الحديثة، بينما يحافظ موسي، الذي كتب التراك وأداه، على حضوره الخاص وسط هذا الصوت المختلف. ويشارك مروان سامي في مرحلة الـMastering، بينما تولى zozrealstar عملية الـMixing، ليخرج التراك في صورة متوازنة تحافظ على تفاصيل الإنتاج وحيويته.

بصريًا، يأخذ المخرج عبدالرحمن المرسي الأغنية إلى عالم مختلف، متخيلًا موسي وحيدًا وسط المدينة، في مشاهد تهيمن عليها أضواء النيون والمساحات الليلية. ولا يكتفي هذا العالم البصري بمرافقة الموسيقى، بل يعكس حالة الوحدة والصراع التي يدور حولها التراك، ويمنحه هوية بصرية مميزة تكمل صوته الموسيقي.

## Katherine Yeske Taylor

**Katherine Yeske Taylor** is a longtime New Yorker, but she began her rock critic career in Atlanta in the 1990s, interviewing Georgia musical royalty such as **Indigo Girls**, **R.E.M.** and **The Black Crowes** while she was still a teenager. Since then, she has conducted thousands of interviews with a wide range of artists for dozens of national, regional, and local magazines and newspapers, including _Billboard_, _Spin_, _American Songwriter_, _FLOOD_, etc. She is the author of two books: She’s a Badass: Women in Rock Shaping Feminism_ (published in 2024 via **Backbeat Books**), and she’s currently helping **Eugene Hütz** of **Gogol Bordello** write his memoir, _Rock the Hützpah: Undestructible Ukrainian in the Free World_ (out in 2025 via **Matt Holt Books/BenBella**). She also contributed to two prestigious music books, _Rolling Stone’s Alt-Rock-A-Rama_ and _The Trouser Press Guide to ’90s Rock_. She has written album liner notes and artist bios (PR materials) for several major musical artists.

by [Jeff Alexander](https://bigtakeover.com/author/Jeff+Alexander/)

“I always make sure to stay busy writing. At one point, I was writing for DrugLords of The Avenues, Swingin’ Utters, and our side project, Filthy Thieving Bastards at the same time. I didn’t feel overwhelmed because it allowed me to continue exploring different styles,” said Bonnel.

3 October 2025

by [S.W. Lauden](https://bigtakeover.com/author/S.W.+Lauden/)

The music gods continue to smile down on power pop fans in 2025, but the gifts they bestow aren’t always obvious. Featuring Liquid Mike, Strange Magic, Lùlù, Dots, and Softjaw.

26 September 2025

by [Jeff Alexander](https://bigtakeover.com/author/Jeff+Alexander/)

“The ethos remains within me because I learned early on that the music was a driving force for change, either for individual change or within communities. No matter how young I was, I always gravitated to the community, and starting Strange Club Records enabled me to create relationships with people from all over,” said Hanover.

“I used that same DIY energy to help people tell important stories that made them who they are today, and that keeps the subculture strong. Turning a profit is not always as important as creating this avenue for people, and I feel it has given DiWulf a special meaning,” said Wuelfing.

# Bu Nasser Touffar On Resistance & The Shared Struggle of Arabs

The Lebanese rapper breaks down the philosophy behind his music and how it reflects the political climate in the region.

[Riham Issa](https://scenenoise.com/WriterProfile/5286)

Sep 18, 2026

![Image 6: Bu Nasser Touffar On Resistance & The Shared Struggle of Arabs ](https://scenenoise.com/Content/Articles/Big_image/bd25a2ce-ec2f-49ff-97b9-68594c3dd0b8.jpg)

Hailing from Lebanon’s historically neglected Bekaa Valley, Bu Nasser Touffar remains one of the Arab underground’s most uncompromising voices. Ever since emerging as part of seminal hip-hop duo Touffar in the late 2000s, the rapper, novelist, and lyricist has steadfastly refused to sanitise his narrative for palatable mainstream consumption. Speaking at Oakenfest 2026, Touffar framed his work as an intentional counterweight to the political and cultural forces dividing collective struggles across the region.

At the core of Touffar’s ethos is a sharp critique of power structures that weaponise isolation. Authoritarian regimes throughout Lebanon, Syria, Egypt, and beyond maintain control by convincing populations that their grievances are distinct and localised. Touffar counters this by treating regional suffering as a singular, interconnected experience against systemic oppression and military occupation, using his music to forge a shared vernacular across manufactured borders.

This commitment to restoring humanity to political violence culminates in his track ‘The Others.’ Facing a media landscape where the genocide committed by Israel in Palestine routinely flattens Palestinian lives into transient statistics, Touffar re-anchors the narrative around individual names, faces, and stolen futures. It is an exercise in active memory against erasure, rooted in the clear-eyed conviction that while entire homes and lineages have been destroyed, the survivors vastly outnumber the fallen and will outlast the occupation.

Navigating both literature and rap, Touffar adapts his technique to the medium while keeping his core purpose fixed. Where prose offers boundless structural freedom, hip-hop enforces strict cadences, rhythms, and rhyme schemes. Yet both disciplines serve the same non-negotiable imperative: defending the oppressed. Crucially, he shuns preachy sloganeering, treating music as a multi-layered craft that listeners can continually revisit and unpack over time.

In a region steeped in dark, absurd brutality, Touffar redefines resistance not as abstract rhetoric, but as a daily practice of preserving ethics, humanity, and creative autonomy. His trajectory as an independent artist mirrors the endurance of millions holding onto their dignity against overwhelming odds, ensuring his work remains an unyielding testament to survival.

### [Interview: Maoli](https://bigtakeover.com/interviews/interview-maoli)

[![Image 10](https://bigtakeover.com/images/37911.jpg)](https://bigtakeover.com/images/37911.jpg)

29 August 2026

by [Katherine Yeske Taylor](https://bigtakeover.com/author/Katherine+Yeske+Taylor/)

Photo by Sean McGee

Anyone who has visited the Hawaiian islands has likely encountered “Jawaiian,” the musical style that is unique to that place. Blending reggae, country, and a breezy vibe, it is feel-good music that perfectly embodies Hawaii’s laid-back atmosphere and locals’ upbeat attitude. For the past fifteen years, one of the leading artists in this genre is **Maoli**, whose 2008 debut album, _Groovin_, immediately became a hit in Hawaii. Across several more albums, Maoli’s success expanded to mainland North America and throughout the Pacific, thanks to hits such as “Every Night Every Morning,” “You Can Have It All,” “Mercy,” “Beautiful,” and many more.

In 2025, Maoli switched to full-on country with the album _Last Sip of Summer_, which resulted in a debut appearance at the **Grand Ole Opry**. Now, though, there’s a return to the blend of reggae and island country with _MMO 3_, which was just put out on August 28. It is the final installment in a trilogy that began with _Maoli Music Overload_, then _MMO2_, both released in 2023.

Calling from Maui, Maoli explains to _The Big Takeover_ about his unique sound, how hard work at a string of difficult jobs makes him appreciate his success in music, and why he thinks his music has connected with listeners throughout Hawaii and beyond.

_For someone who hasn’t been exposed to your music yet, can you give an overview of what your vibe is, and what you’re aiming to do with your music?_

MAOLI: When you come to the [Hawaiian] islands, you get to really experience the culture, and also the music, and it’s a style and a way of thinking that is different than any place in the world. For me, growing up in Hawaii, there was a lot of country living. A lot of people don’t know that, when it comes to the islands. A lot of people think that we’re just people living in huts and stuff like that, living off the land! [laughs] But no, there’s a lot of country living out here. So I got to relate to a lot of artists growing up, like **George Jones** and **Vince Gill** and **George Strait** – I had country music embedded in me from a young age. This is kind of a mixture of country and reggae, so it’s the storytelling and the melodies of country, but yet the island feel of the reggae, mixed together. The reggae comes from Jamaica, but one thing that Jamaica and Hawaii have in common is, we’re both island people. So having this mixture together is kind of describing our sound.

![Image 11](https://bigtakeover.com/images/37913.png)
_Congratulations on your new album. How do you feel as it’s being released into the world?_

MAOLI: I feel good. It’s an ending of an era for me. _MMO 1_ [_Maoli Music Overload_, released in 2023] was pretty much my most successful album to date, so ending this whole era is a cool thing for me. It’s just something I wanted to seal up and start something new. I just knew that I had to kind of put an end to this, and we’ll see what the future has to hold.

_You did start something new with your last album already, with your focus on country music…_

MAOLI: Yeah, for sure. That was a fun project that I got to do in Nashville with [producer] **Dan Huff**. It was a fun experience. It was really different, but I still had fun doing it.

_When you first started out, did you have this sound in mind?_

MAOLI: It didn’t start like that. I started off in Hawaiian music and reggae, and then, as I got older, I started playing music and doing a lot of shows here and there. It kind of grew on me where, being from the country, I wanted to go back to where I came from, and it just fell into place.

_What’s the music scene like in Hawaii?_

MAOLI: I like to say we have our own industry. Something similar to Nashville, but on a smaller scale. But our industry here, you can make a really good living here doing music. I think we’re the second highest in the world with weddings, so we do a lot of weddings here, we do a lot of graduation parties. You can actually tour just in the Pacific, as far as Tahiti, Hawaii, New Zealand and stuff like that.

_Is it hard to break into the scene there?_

MAOLI: Yes and no. Maybe for some others, it might be a little hard. But for our local artists, it’s not too hard. We’re very supportive of our artists.

[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SN3LzYCamb4)

_What made you want to be a professional musician in the first place?_

MAOLI: I just always knew it was my calling in my life. It’s just something I honestly could never get away from. I tried other jobs, and it seemed like I couldn’t hold a job for longer than two months. It always just led me straight back to music. As I started recording and releasing music and started playing shows in the beginning of my career, I kind of knew that, “Maybe I’m good at this.” I guess the fans that love my music, they really stuck around.

_What were the other jobs you tried?_

MAOLI: Oh, man. I did carpentry, concrete, masonry. I was a dishwasher. I worked in farms and stuff like that. A lot of labor jobs. Very hard jobs. That’s why when music found me, I was pretty stoked to do it.

_Of course, many people say they want to be a professional musician, but then it turns out they don’t have the talent or the drive. How did you discover that you do?_

MAOLI: It comes from that background of hard work. Even before I had a real job, I was always working at home on my grandpa’s farm. I always had chores. Throughout my life, I always knew what hard work was, so when it came to the music industry, it can be difficult sometimes, but to me, it always felt like it wasn’t as hard as farming and stuff like that. I’d rather be doing music all day than being in the hot sun. So it kind of helped me deal with all the stuff that comes with the industry where it can be difficult. Being on the road away from your family, there’s a lot of sacrifice that people don’t understand that is required when it comes to being a musician. Some people say they want to be a musician, until they really start to understand the sacrifice that is required when it comes to becoming a successful artist.

_When did you start learning to play the guitar and learning to sing?_

MAOLI: I would kind of say I was a natural drummer, so I picked up drums at a young age. My father bought me my first drum set, I believe, when I was four or five years old, and I started playing on that. As I got into intermediate school, here in Hawaii, it’s almost like you _have_ to play ukulele, so there were classes in school that you had to take where they were teaching you ukulele. And as I did ukulele, you get into other instruments, too: guitar, bass, these other instruments. But I really started when I was playing drums, and it just kind of led from there.

[Video 2](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZPId1j90fnU)

_Do you remember the first song you ever wrote?_

MAOLI: I do, and I don’t like to talk about that because I sucked at it! [laughs]

_Well, everybody starts somewhere!_

MAOLI: It’s funny because my 8th grade year, there was this class called “Polynesian Music” where, at the end of the year, in order to get your final grade, you had to write a song, and you had to perform it in front of the class. I remember how, Oh my God, I was so nervous to do this because I didn’t like to sing in front of people. I was very shy. Not only am I shy, “Now I’ve got to write a song and sing it, Oh my God” – it was torture for me. Anyway, my teacher retired, [but] he was very proud that he had a student that got some success with music, so he would play that video for all the students. He played it for maybe at least thirty years.

_Do you remember when you realized music was going to work out for you as a career and you wouldn’t have to go back to those other kinds of jobs?_

MAOLI: It’s an ongoing thing. It was maybe only about four or five years ago that I really, really started to find success in music. But I would say fifteen years before that, I didn’t know if I was going to do this for a living or not. There was a lot of grinding involved. But it wasn’t until _MMO_, I would say, where my career just really blossomed in the Pacific and the West Coast, mostly. That’s why this ending of an era, if you want to call it that, I’m just proud of it because it’s like the ending of this – this was the start of my career where I really blew up, and now that I had my fun, I want to do some different things.

_What do you think might come next?_

MAOLI: I would say the music won’t change a lot, but it’s going to have its different feel, but the roots of my music will always stay the same.

_It seems like a lot of artists run out of ideas after a while, but you seem quite prolific. How do you stay inspired?_

MAOLI: I like to experience things in life. I think with anyone, you go through ups and downs in life, and you can use that when it comes to the creativity, because to me, I just feel like you start to understand what it’s like to be human. I just want to give these people, my fans, an experience. I go out there and I experience life, and I get inspired by not only myself, but other people that inspire me with their stories and walks in life.

[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iUo3Ra55TXI)

_What do you think it is about your music that has made it connect so strongly with so many listeners?_

MAOLI: I think it’s just me being me, I guess. I like to think of it as, if you do love the music, it’s really just a reflection of who you are. So if you can relate to it, you’ll love it, no matter if you’re white, Black, Hawaiian, Polynesian, no matter what.

_I see you’ve done some recent shows. Will you do a more extensive North American tour for this album?_

MAOLI: This year, I’ve been taking it easy because I’m always in the studio, I’m always writing and trying to make music. So this year, I wanted to take it easy on the road, so I haven’t been touring as much. But next year, yes, I will be doing a lot of shows. 2027 and 2028, we’re going to be doing markets I’ve never done before, such as Europe or Brazil, so it’s really exciting.

_What do you think about the legacy you’ve created so far with your career?_

# Tamino on Mythology, Egypt’s Charm & The Soulful Essence of ‘Sahar’

Right at the end of his ‘Sahar’ tour, SceneNoise sat down for an exclusive interview with Belgian-Egyptian singer-songwriter Tamino in Cairo.

[Ziyad El-Helbawy](https://scenenoise.com/WriterProfile/5296)

Sep 13, 2025

![Image 6: Tamino on Mythology, Egypt’s Charm & The Soulful Essence of ‘Sahar’](https://scenenoise.com/Content/Articles/Big_image/3ac91d46-4f5a-444c-9711-3a8bdee9af02.jpg)

_Cover Photo courtesy of Cairo Zoom_

_“Nice to meet you, etsharaft… is that right? I’m still working on my Arabic.”_

So went my first interaction with Tamino.

On Friday the 22nd of September, at approximately 2:47 PM, a few hours before what would be the penultimate night of his ‘Sahar’ tour, I walk up the staircase at the Hill House at the American University in Cairo. After a right turn, I then take the elevator three floors up. The door opens, and I take a step ahead inside a vast and empty conference hall and wait… Soon enough, the door opens, and in walks the Belgian-Egyptian singer-songwriter, Tamino-Amir Muharram Fouad.

Fresh off the plane following his shows in Turkey, Tamino was about to end his introspective and soulful ‘Sahar’ tour on the album’s first-year anniversary in a country that he, his father, and his father’s father hold dear: Egypt.

I had the privilege and pleasure of sitting down with Tamino for an exclusive SceneNoise interview in a warm and laidback encounter that wholly discredits anyone who might utter the words, “Don’t meet your idols.” During our conversation, the artist spoke of life, inspiration, music, memories…and his love for Lord of the Rings and stuffed pigeons.

**![Image 7](https://scenenow.com/Content/editor_api/images/Website%20copy%209%20(2)-435f6c59-df22-474e-b80d-d042f6e5bdbb.jpg)_Photo Credit: Aleksei Benuchi_**

**It’s so very nice to meet you! Welcome back!**

Nice to meet you, etsharaft… is that right? I’m still working on my Arabic.

**I see those Arabic Duolingo classes are going well.**

Oh I'm using another app now, Pimsleur! I actually should get on it more often…

**How was your flight?**

It was alright! Just four hours, not that long…the thing is though, the plane looked like it was from the nineties. Kind of funny looking.

How was Istanbul? How was the tour so far?

It’s been very good. The shows in Turkey and Egypt are definitely the biggest adventures of the tour I feel. All the other shows have been in regions we’re kind of used to, especially for the band, most of whom have never even been to Egypt before. They’re excited and I’m excited to bring them here.

Like any tour, there are some shows you’ll like and some not as much, it’s hard to predict. It’s like you can’t predict whether you’re gonna have a good day or a bad day. I try to meditate to prepare; I would say it all comes down to one’s state of presence. If I'm in the moment, I can just enjoy the music, the crowds, and just really immerse myself - those are the best shows I would say.

There were times where I was completely lost in thought, and that is when I get very very critical of my own writing, even while I’m playing them up on stage.“I could’ve written this better,” I might think sometimes. Those are the worst moments on stage.

**So are you getting good vibes from tonight’s show?**

Oh of course! From the moment we announced it, we could just feel the excitement and we were honoured. I’m excited and I’m curious to see how it goes…

**Do you have any post-show plans set yet?**

Oh I definitely wanna bring the band to Khan El Khalili. Some of them haven’t even seen the pyramids yet! Cairo is just so big…I’d love to go to Dahab, but it’s just so far. I just love the Red Sea. Sinai is such a spiritual place.

**Obviously music runs in the family - your grandfather is quite the beloved man here in Egypt - what would you say your earliest musical memory was?**

Hmm…It’s hard to pin down just one, but it’s probably my mother playing the piano. That was always a thing around the house; come morning or evening, she would always be playing these brilliant classical pieces, and when she wasn’t, there were always records playing around the house. Arabic, Jazz, classical…it was a whole lot of everything.

**![Image 8](https://scenenow.com/Content/editor_api/images/Website%20copy%2010-87321ce5-1ca4-4a5f-84c8-3ddb8b9cd066.jpg)_Photo Credit: Herman Selleslags_**

**On the topic of memories, what kind of future did little Tamino imagine for himself? Did you think you’d one day be out here touring the world?**

Well, actually, here’s a fun story. I wanted to be a film director, and I’d probably say that’s because of Lord of the Rings. I’m such a huge fan of the series and that world. I remember my grandmother had hidden the VCR tape because she just knew that once I saw ‘Lord of the Rings’ on the cover I would just grab it and just keep watching non-stop. One time I saw the video lying atop the cupboard so I just took a chair, grabbed it, and watched everything till they got back home. Ramy was with me, he was probably traumatised by what he was seeing. Poor five-year-old.

Ever since then, I have had a very vivid imagination. I was always making these little theatre plays and bossing my brother around to play the parts I'd tell him to play. I’d ask my mom and grandparents to watch the plays I'd come up with. I just knew I was a storyteller and I always envisioned myself to be a director one day. I even went to acting school, and it was a lot of fun, but I'm quite introverted, so the moment I found out that I could create something entirely by myself - which was music - I decided to pursue that. I wrote my first song at 14.

**And is that the one you always refuse to talk about?**

(Laughs) Oh I never will. That song is buried. Buried alive.

**I would sell my soul to listen to it now…**

You’d definitely want it back! (Laughs) It was a really… shitty song, but the feeling it gave me was truly unlike any feeling I’d had before. I realised I could do it all by myself. I could write, I could play it, or I could keep it for myself, which I did. To me, I feel like that’s the best way for me to create stuff; that solitary phase to me is my favourite place to be, mentally.

Of course the entire process can’t be solitary. But still, those initial creative sparks, that safe space in the end is why music won. Being back in that space is what I miss when I’m on tour, and is what I look forward to.

**And what is that space like? How would you describe your creative process? What part of you do the songs stem from?**

I really don’t know. I’d say the process is actually very banal. It’s just me with an instrument, a guitar, a piano, or even an oud now. Just me playing and noodling until I find something that moves me. It’s very much how you would imagine it goes.

**Would you say the songs come piece by piece?**

Oh definitely. One spark leads to another. It’s quite rare to have a song present itself in full format. That has maybe happened to me two or three times, but almost always they come one line at a time.

**Which songs would you say are the ones that came to you fully realised?**

‘The Longing’, definitely. ‘Indigo Night’ I’d say as well. ‘Tummy’, maybe?

**I love Tummy’s music video!**

It’s so funny! Do you see the humour in it? We just wanted to make something fun and I’m proud of it.

**[Video 1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HB6JjgEubrk)Another song I love of yours is ‘Persephone’. I just love Greek Mythology and I have to ask, what are your literary influences? What inspires you?**

I don’t know what draws me to a book, but I’ve always loved mythology and stories. I feel like a lot of these stories often have metaphysical truths to them that are just very inherent to being a human being. Even in fantasies, the lessons and the morals are still there. These truths that are touched upon in literature are often more difficult to touch upon in reality, and that’s why I love stories.

Magical realism is also something that I love, like what we did with the music video for ‘Indigo Night’, I would say that borders on magical realism. I love playing with that genre; in my lyrics, music videos, and in my storytelling as a whole. The last book I read was actually in the magical realism genre, called ‘The Gargoyle’. It’s about this man who gets burnt and no longer wants to live, and then this woman who claims to have seen him for centuries walks into his hospital room and just falls in love with him. It’s this weird love story where you never truly know what’s happening, it’s thought-provoking and I love those kinds of stories. They’re beautiful.

**![Image 9](https://scenenow.com/Content/editor_api/images/Website%20copy%207%20(6)-4982c960-aa63-449c-ac44-1c603c4d8659.jpg)_Photo Credit: Herman Selleslags_**

**Speaking of beautiful, you’re playing the oud now! How does that feel? Is it different from the guitar - in the sense that you feel more connected to your Arabic roots?**

For sure. It’s gotten to a point now where I feel like I can play the oud in my own way. At first, I just really wanted to be respectful of the traditions. It’s not like the guitar where you can just play outside the rules. I feel like for the oud, there’s a heritage to it you must first understand. I’m still far from a master oud player, but now I can go a bit further and so I’m at a point where I can do something that feels very intuitive with the oud, something that makes me feel connected to my roots, without it feeling forced. It just feels so liberating. It just flows. It connects to the spirit. It truly is the instrument of the soul.

**I can definitely feel that connection when I listen to ‘A Drop of Blood’ - are you playing that tonight?**

It’s actually the first song! And we actually have our oud teacher Tarek with us, and he’s incredible. We’re going to be playing a few songs with the oud together, including a new one.

**Ooh, is that perhaps part of an upcoming album, maybe?**

I hope! I usually write a bunch of songs, and a lot of them don’t make it on the album. Some I tend to not like after a while. I do think that the one I'm playing tonight might make it on the album. I wrote the base of it in New York last winter, and I still like the song, so it looks promising.

**So I’ve heard you’re planning on moving to New York! How do you feel?**

Yes, in two weeks! I feel slightly frightened but quite excited. I think I only have a guitar at home there, I really need to get a mattress soon. (Laughs)

**‘Sahar’ was written mostly in the pandemic - what would ‘Sahar’ look like today if the pandemic had never happened?**

It would not have been the same. Looking back, it’s pretty much a pandemic record. So many so-called ‘lockdown’ albums at the time were coming out, and I didn’t want mine to be a part of that. But looking back at it now, it’s pretty much heavily pandemic-influenced. It’s quite reflective and introspective. We all had time to reflect on our lives then, you could literally feel it in the air. For me, that period of introspection was quite needed following the roller coaster my life had taken me on the year before. It was insane how drastically my life had changed at that point, it was a much needed break. So yeah, ‘Sahar’ wouldn’t have been ‘Sahar’ had it not been for the pandemic.

‘Amir’ came at a time of live performances, and so it’s more dramatic. I’d say ‘Amir’ was directly influenced by all the big shows we were doing at the time. For ‘Sahar’, I didn’t have that sense of ‘drama,’ it was much calmer.

**I know it’s hard to pick favourites, but what are some of your top songs from both albums?**

It’s hard to pick a favourite but the top _songs_ I can definitely do. I’d say ‘Indigo Night’ is one - it’s a song I always love performing. ‘Habibi’ definitely is another, it’s a song I’ve played a lot and never tire of. I really sense the impact of it on people. From ‘Sahar’, I’d say ‘The Longing’.

With some songs I have a love-hate relationship, which I would say is quite normal with anything in life that one creates. I see that as a positive thing because it drives you forward. If you’re content with everything you make, you won’t feel the need to better yourself. You can use those negative feelings to push yourself forward.

I hope one day I’ll be at a place where I find peace of mind looking back at all my work. But I’m proud of everything.

**Where do you think life will take you? In a few years perhaps…**

If I just look at my whole life so far, all of it has been guided by a longing for freedom. Just freedom from myself, my own mind. I just want to do a whole lot of meditating. Another way to freedom I would say is through my creative work; when things really started taking off in my career, I felt kind of constrained, the pressure of having to do all these shows, and I still sometimes feel that pressure and I want to get to a point where I don't feel that. That’s where I want life to take me. I would like to slow down a little bit, that slowness of life is what feeds me and feeds my creativity.

At some point, I want to come to Egypt. Every time I’m here in Egypt I’m like, “Fuck, I need to spend more time here.” It’s a dream that I have at one point to spend more time in Cairo or maybe Sinai if a spiritual journey calls. Egypt just feels right. I cannot explain it, but there’s something logical about being in Egypt. There’s a connection I feel, to the people even. It always means a lot to me coming here. And I can’t wait for more adventures here.

**![Image 10](https://scenenow.com/Content/editor_api/images/Website%20copy%2011%20(1)-e8b2c856-cadc-4ff8-978f-b9b11b7b1bc8.jpg)_Photo Credit: Ramy Muharram Fouad_**

**Your brother has been accompanying you throughout the tour, how does that feel? What’s your relationship like now that you’re working together all the time?**

It’s great. We have a wonderful relationship as brothers and as colleagues. He’s a brilliant photographer. I do think that after ‘Amir’, there was a time where we worked on everything with each other. I mean it’s brilliant working together, but it may not always be the best creative choice being constantly dependent on one another. So we had to sit down and have a talk, and came to an agreement that when we do work together, it’s because we both want to.

**The last leg of the Sahar tour is here! Do you have any post-tour plans?**

I’m just in a rush to get everything ready for New York! I’ll probably be busy with all the practicals. But once I'm in New York - and once I get that mattress (Laughs) - then I'll be good to go.

**Have you considered singing in Arabic one day?**

Definitely. I mean I could sing in Arabic now, but I would have to learn the song phonetically and I wouldn’t feel the lyrics as much as I wanna feel them, so I wanna avoid that for now. I need to learn to speak it first so I can sing it.

**Okay so, rapid-fire round. Ready?**

Let’s go.

**If you could collaborate with any late artist, who would it be?**

Since we’re in Egypt, Riad Al Sunbati.

**And who would you collaborate with today?**

A dear friend who recently passed away, Tom Pintens, who actually produced my first EP, always said I should work with Alberto Iglesias. It’s something he always told me, and now with his passing, I've thought of it a lot. I love his music.

**Sunrise or sunset?**

Definitely sunrise. I’m a morning person.

**Favourite Egyptian dish?**

Probably stuffed pigeons, I like them!

**Favourite movie?**

Lord of the Rings. Always.

**Favourite memory?**

When I was in Dahab with my mother at 14. It was beautiful and I was mesmerised.

I cannot wait to make new Egyptian memories.

_And with that, our conversation ends. Tamino gets up, heads to soundcheck, and prepares to hypnotise a crowd of devoted fans._

# Tamino Amir's Egyptian Homecoming: The Interview

Upon his first gig in Egypt at CJC 610, we sat down with Tamino Amir where we got to know more about the man behind the mystifying voice.

[Ramy AlMagdoub](https://scenenoise.com/WriterProfile/5195)

Oct 28, 2019

![Image 6: Tamino Amir's Egyptian Homecoming: The Interview](https://scenenoise.com/Content/Articles/Big_image/637077630584409888____.jpg)

Rising to the global indie scene with his otherworldly hit single 'Habibi' in 2017, 22-year-old Egyptian Belgian singer/songwriter Tamino Amir garnered popularity, awards and international acclaim with his debut full length album _Amir_ that showcased unique, evocative vocal performances, beautifully sullen songwriting and visually captivating videos. Hailing from a musically prestigious namesake, Tamino is the grandson of Egyptian singer and movie star Muharram Fouad who was known as The Voice of The Nile during the Golden Age of Egyptian cinema.<iframe src="https://www.facebook.com/plugins/video.php?href=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.facebook.com%2FSceneNoise%2Fvideos%2F718650285320317%2F&show_text=0&width=560" width="560" height="315" style="border:none;overflow:hidden" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" allowTransparency="true" allowFullScreen="true"></iframe>Ever since breaking out into the international arena, Tamino has been paving the way for himself and his career equally - Working and touring with the likes of Radiohead's bassist Colin Greenwood, all the while, opening up for Lana Del Rey's Dublin show in 2018 and as of lately performing for the first time in the US with four shows at 2019's SXSW. Tamino has also been making headlines in the fashion world - gracing the pages of Vogue Hommes while appearing alongside international supermodel Gisele Bündchen in Missoni's SS20 campaign, marking him as a man of many talents. We got to speak to indie music's rising star in light of his first gig in his home country at Cairo Jazz Club 610 - Here's what he had to say.
